Newborn Care

Recognizing Illness in a Newborn: When to Call the Doctor

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited by Mohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama — checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

New parents often worry about overreacting. With newborns, the medical world takes the opposite view: call early and call often. Young babies cannot tell you what is wrong and can change quickly, so care teams genuinely want to hear from you. Here are the signs that always deserve a call.

Fever in a newborn is always a call

In babies under about three months, fever is treated as urgent — a rectal temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher means contact your doctor or seek medical care right away, even if your baby seems okay otherwise, and even in the middle of the night.

Do not try to manage a newborn fever at home or wait to see how it develops; young infants need prompt evaluation. A temperature notably below normal in a baby who seems off is also worth an urgent call.

Feeding refusal and dehydration signs

A newborn who refuses several feeds in a row, feeds much more weakly than usual, or is too sleepy to eat needs a call to the doctor. Small dips in appetite happen, but a real pattern of not feeding is a warning sign in this age group.

Watch the diapers for dehydration: significantly fewer wet diapers than usual, dark or strong-smelling urine, a dry mouth, no tears when crying, or a sunken soft spot on the head. Any of these in a newborn warrants prompt medical advice.

Breathing that does not look right

Newborns are naturally noisy, irregular breathers, so the key is effort, not sound. Warning signs include very fast breathing that persists, grunting with each breath, flaring nostrils, the skin pulling in between or below the ribs, or long pauses in breathing.

Blue or gray color around the lips, tongue, or face is an emergency — seek emergency care immediately. For any breathing effort concerns, it is always right to call rather than watch and wait.

Jaundice to keep an eye on

Mild yellowing of the skin and eyes is common in the first days and often resolves as feeding gets established. Your care team will usually check it before and after you leave the hospital.

Call your provider if the yellow color deepens or spreads down the belly, arms, or legs, if it appears in the first day of life, or if your jaundiced baby is very sleepy, feeding poorly, or hard to wake. Jaundice is very treatable, but the significant cases need timely care.

Lethargy and just seeming "off"

Newborns sleep a lot, but they should wake for feeds and have alert periods. A baby who is unusually floppy, hard to rouse, uninterested in feeding, or crying weakly — or one whose cry is high-pitched and unusual — needs prompt medical attention.

Trust your instincts here. Parents notice "something is different" before they can name it, and clinicians take that seriously. You know your baby’s normal better than anyone.

Calling early is the right call

Pediatric teams plan for worried-parent calls — they are a designed part of newborn care, not an imposition. No one will fault you for a call that turns out to be nothing; that is the best possible outcome.

Keep your provider’s daytime number, after-hours line, and the local emergency number saved in your phone before you need them. When you do call, notes on temperature, feeds, and diaper counts help the conversation go quickly.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

A rectal temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher in a baby three months or younger requires immediate medical contact, even when the baby otherwise appears well. Young infants can have serious infection without many obvious symptoms.

Breathing difficulty, blue or grey colour, marked sleepiness, seizures, persistent vomiting, dehydration, poor feeding, or a rapidly changing rash also require urgent assessment.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to record the exact temperature, method, time, feeding, diapers, and symptoms while arranging care. Do not wait for a trend or AI response before calling.

When to seek help

Call the baby’s clinician or urgent service immediately for fever in a young infant; use emergency services for severe breathing, responsiveness, colour, or seizure concerns.

Sources and further reading

  • American Academy of Pediatrics — Fever and Your Baby

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Fever of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher in a baby under 3 months means contact a doctor right away.
  • Repeated feeding refusal or fewer wet diapers than usual deserve a prompt call.
  • Labored breathing — grunting, flaring, ribs pulling in — needs urgent attention; blue lips are an emergency.
  • Deepening or spreading jaundice, especially with sleepiness or poor feeding, needs timely care.
  • Calling early is always right — care teams expect and welcome newborn calls.

Frequently asked questions

What counts as a fever in a newborn?

A rectal temperature of 38°C (100.4°F) or higher. In a baby under about three months, that always means contacting a doctor or seeking care promptly rather than treating it at home.

Will the doctor mind if it turns out to be nothing?

No — a false alarm is the best outcome, and pediatric teams build their days around exactly these calls. With newborns, the standing advice is to call early rather than wait.

How can I tell normal newborn noises from breathing trouble?

Newborns snuffle and breathe irregularly, which is normal. Concerning signs are about effort: persistent fast breathing, grunting, nostril flaring, skin pulling in around the ribs, or any blue or gray coloring — those need immediate attention.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
